en: The Gadā Parva (The Book of the Club)
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Victory! (Jaya).
Then three heroic warriors, led by the son of Droṇa, approached and addressed the king—who was rich in honor and had entered the lake—with their arrows: Bhājya 10.2.
"O King, arise in battle and slay the enemy, O wielder of the bow!
Together with us, this is the time for valor that brings forth glory."
Having heard this, the Lord of the Kurus, praising his prowess, said after consoling him: "In the morning, my course shall be such as is fitting for a warrior."
Having heard this conversation of theirs and having recognized Suyodhana,
the hunters, greedy for wealth, informed Bhīmasena.
Then, at the word of Bhīmasena, King Yudhiṣṭhira, together with his army and accompanied by those headed by Kṛṣṇa, quickly arrived at that place.
Seeing the sons of Pṛthā arrived with their armies of roaring elephants and chariots,
Gautama and the others departed out of fear of being implicated as informers to the king.
Then, at the word of Kṛṣṇa, that best of kings, the son of Dharma, spoke to Suyodhana who was situated within the waters.
O King!
Alas, O hero, your bright fame—so beautiful as silver, camphor, and the moon—has been defiled by you.
Having caused kings— who were the very abodes of the lineage of Fortune— to be slain in battle,
how is it that you, a proud man intent only on saving your own life, do not feel shame while still living?
Arise for battle and attain your own glory or the third heaven;
for among heroes, victory or death are indeed equal.
Having heard these words of Yudhiṣṭhira, Duryodhana, overwhelmed by the poison of wrath,
spoke while hissing like an elephant stuck in the mud.
"It is exactly as you say; for me, prosperity is indeed the same as death.
But whose mind would be touched by fortune when it is devoid of kinsmen and relatives?"
Whose mind is gladdened by an army bereft of heroes, like a social gathering devoid of the wise, or by fortune separated from one's own kin? (Bhājana 10.14)
He was the foremost of friends, he was a teacher, he was a grandfather; alas, whose memory would not fail him, even that of a great sage, were it not for the forest of asceticism? (Bhājana 10.15)
For those separated from kinsmen and friends, worldly prosperities are indeed a mockery,
like variegated paintings of beauty before the blind.
Enjoy the earth, already tasted by me, which is devoid of heroes as its jewels—
like an aged woman whose ornaments have been stripped away by dispassion.
Having heard this, the son of Pṛthā spoke to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"By good fortune, O Lord of the Earth, you have become peaceful and have set your heart upon the forest of asceticism."
Not even a needle's point of this earth should be surrendered by you to the Pāṇḍavas;
yet today you desire to give away the entire world out of curiosity.
"Arise and fight with one man; if he is conquered by you, O King, then all have been conquered by you. Do not become emaciated with idle talk. (Bhājana 10.20)
Upon hearing these words of Pārtha, the king rose up in anger;
for those possessed of pride cannot endure being addressed with haughty speech. (Bhājana 10.21)
With golden armlets and mace in hand, that king rose up like Mount Sumeru with its peaks, appearing like another wielder of the staff of punishment.
At Kṛṣṇa’s word, Vṛkodara, mace in hand and fully armored, stood before him,
intent on enumerating Draupadī’s sufferings.

***** The Appearance of Duryodhana // 1 // ***** In the meantime, Haladhara (Balarāma), distressed by the fear of the destruction of his kinsmen during the slaughter of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, arrived slowly on a pilgrimage to the sacred fords. Bhājya 10.24.
Then, having arrived at Kurukṣetra, he beheld those two armed with maces,
watching the combat between his two disciples as if listening to their mutual conversation.
Honored by the sons of Pṛthā, led by Kṛṣṇa, he— possessing the luster of a hundred moons and clad in blue garments—
sat down like the Himavat mountain with its clouds.
Having heard these words at the beginning of the story, Janamejaya respectfully asked Vaiśampāyana about the pilgrimage of the wielder of the plow (Balarāma).
When the battle between the Kuru and Pāṇḍava kings was about to commence,
he (Bhīma) took leave of Kṛṣṇa and departed, fearing for his own life, while the slayer of Pralamba remained behind.
Having departed from Puṣpa, Rāma, who grants all desires, reached Sarasvatī; then, by means of his sacrificial bed, he proceeded to Prabhāsa.
There, Tārā, becoming distressed, reported to her father that the Lord of Stars (the Moon) was intent on Rohiṇī; because of his curse, he became consumptive.
In an instant, when the moon had been wasted away by consumption due to the curse,
the gods, agitated by the fear of universal destruction, then departed as directed by fate.
Laughing, he quickly reached fullness even there by that radiance;
having bathed there with great devotion, Vajra proceeded to Tritakūpa.
Where formerly King Trita was neglected by his two brothers, he performed a mental sacrifice; thereupon the gods arrived.
Then, by virtue of that boon, a well appeared which bestowed the fruit of drinking the Soma;
on that bank of the Sarasvatī, Rāma stayed there with great devotion.
From there he reached the meritorious Vinaśana, where the Sarasvatī—
feared by Śūdras, hated by the ignorant, and the destroyer of the wicked— disappears.
Then that powerful one proceeded to that region where the gods and gandharvas, accompanied by apsarases, sport with the diversions of dance and song.
Having reached Durgasrotas, Śaṅkhatīrtha, the meritorious Dvaitavana, as well as Nagadhanvan, where Vāsuki has his dwelling; Bhmj_10.37.
Rāma entered Naimiṣa, where the Sarasvatī flows toward the east,
and where there is the vision of the sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest.
He proceeded to Sapta-sārasvata, where the sage Caṅkaṇaka danced upon seeing vegetable juice flowing from his own body.
As that sage danced with agitation and playfulness in that excellent grove,
the entire world danced as well through the power of his asceticism.
Then, requested by the gods, he approached; because of his sight of Śambara, the ash that had issued from his own hand caused the sage to become free from pride.
Pleased with him who had offered praise, the omnipresent Lord Śaṅkara granted him an increase in ascetic power and his own presence at the Saptasārasvata tīrtha.
Balarāma reached the Kapālamocana tīrtha of Uśanas,
where the sage Mahodara was liberated from a terrible seizure of his leg.
In former times, it is said that the head of the Rākṣasa Mahodara, severed by the arrow of Rāghava, remained clinging to his own shank as it began to slough off.
Although he had immersed himself in all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*), it was only there that he attained well-being;
having reached Uttaṅka’s hermitage, he found Pṛthūdaka.
There, the sage Kauśika, born of the kṣatriya lineage, formerly attained the state of a brāhmaṇa through the spiritual power of Brahman after having defeated Vasiṣṭha, who had stolen his cow.
There, Rāma, the joy of the Vārṣṇeyas, bestowed abundant wealth;
then, in the Sārasvata grove, where Indra [performed his rites] following the slaying of Namuci.
Released from the agitation caused by the slaughter of a Brahmin, he slowly reached that terrible place;
thereafter, he arrived at Somatīrtha, where a sacrifice was being performed by the one of immortal luster.
Where the great asura named Tāraka was slain by the six-faced one,
he then bathed at Skandābhiṣeka and proceeded to Vahnitīrtha.
There, Anala, who had been extinguished by the curse of Bhṛgu, was restored to life;
and there are Kaubera-tīrtha, Indratīrtha, and Yāmuna-tīrtha, where the elder brother of Acyuta [Balarama] performed his rites.
Having reached the hermitage of Devala, Jaijīṣavya, who was skilled in yoga,
[taught] there where the sage had proclaimed to Devala the all-pervading Brahman.
Then Halāyudha reached the Sārasvata tīrtha, where,
prior to the appearance of Apasmarā, semen had fallen into the water.
By means of that [elixir], Sarasvatī obtained a son from the sage Dadhīca,
once the collection of Dadhīca’s bones had been transformed into a rainbow by Mahendra.
During that drought, his son Sārasvata was sustained by her with meals of fish;
that high-minded son remembered the Vedas.
Then, when the study [of the scriptures] had been forgotten due to being ravaged by famine,
he was requested to become the teacher for all the foremost sages.
Having bathed at that sacred ford, Balarāma went to where, in ancient times,
Sanatkumāra had prepared to abandon her body through asceticism for the sake of heaven.
Nārada said, "Without marriage, there can be no heaven";
thus, she gave her body, to be enjoyed for a single day, to the son of Gālava.
Having assumed a graceful form, he then went to the third heaven;
having bathed and given gifts there at Plakṣaprasravaṇa, he likewise [proceeded].
While slowly visiting various sacred fords along the way, he reached Kārapavana;
there, from Nārada, he heard of the destruction of the kings at Kurukṣetra.
***** The Pilgrimage to Rāmatīrtha // 2 // ***** Then,
questioned by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sañjaya described the battle between Bhīmasena and the proud Kaurava who had been deprived of his chariot. Bhmj_10.60 //
Having gone to Samantapañcaka on foot alone, Suyodhana stood motionless; for the great possess even greater fortitude in times of adversity.
Then Duryodhana said to the son of Dharma and his followers:
"Sitting down, may you all observe the two of us as we fight."
Having heard this, Ajātaśatru, accompanied by the Pāñcāla soldiers and with Kṛṣṇa as his companion, sat down surrounding Halāyudha.
Then, once the battle of words had commenced, the joy of the Kurus, having girded his loins, challenged the swift Bhīma, who held his mace in hand, to combat.
Then, the shower of sparks produced by the blows of their maces created the illusion of shimmering golden ornaments as they whirled in their agitation.
When the sky was filled with gods eager to witness the battle,
a certain bewitching curiosity arose among the celestial damsels.
In the sense of throwing, avoiding, liberation, royal conduct, turning back, running, standing still, being agitated, and being completely agitated; Bhmj 10.67.
Those two heroes, moving with boldness in variegated circles,
struck each other’s sides with a great roar and immense speed.
Then Bhīma, having shaken his mace which resounded like a thunderbolt, whirled it around, whereby a terrible,
rumbling roar arose.
Then Bhīma swiftly hurled that mountain-heavy mace;
though struck, the king remained unshaken, and Bhīma again released his mace.
Once more rendered futile by the king, it fell, shaking the earth.
Then, struck on the surface of his chest by the Kuru prince, Bhīma—
his heart overwhelmed by a swoon— was unconscious of anything for a moment.
Then, while the armies of the Pañcālas and Sṛñjayas were agitated by doubt,
Bhīma slowly regained his composure and struck the king on the side.
Struck by a heavy blow, the lord of the Kauravas fell;
rising quickly and striking back, he threw Bhīma to the ground.
Then, a shower of flowers released by the gods and a succession of shouts of "Well done!"— white with fame— fell upon the head of the son of the Kuru king.
Then, as Bhīmasena rose up and quickly wiped away the blood,
Arjuna asked Hari, "Who among these two is the superior warrior?"
The powerful Bhīma, of terrible prowess, said: "What is being said regarding instruction in mace-fighting? But rather, it concerns the valor displayed in battle."
That effort is seen to belong to the Lord of the Kurus [Duryodhana], not to Bhīmasena;
therefore, Bhīma is not capable of being struck down by a righteous battle.
The Daityas were slain by means of illusion, for those who employ illusion can indeed be killed by illusion;
therefore, let Bhīma bring about the breaking of his thighs through illusion.
Otherwise, King Durjaya, having caused fear in the world, exerted himself with his mace for thirteen years against me, the terrible one. (Bhājana 10.79)
Suyodhana, who is skilled in athletic exertion and moves swiftly upward with great force,
will find it easy to break this great stone pillar by observing its weak points.
When Janārdana had spoken thus, Bhīma hurled that terrifying mace;
the Kuru king, however, leaping over it, struck him.
Then Bhīma, steadying his pain though his body reeled for a moment,
hurled at him his gold-banded mace, intending it as a fatal blow.
Like a female serpent upon a pair of thighs that possess the splendor of magnificent golden ornaments from the god whose weapon is flowers, she fell upon the king.

Then Duryodhana fell, his great joints shattered by the crushing impact of the mace with its thunderous sound like a violent storm-cloud; he looked toward the sky like the king of mountains whose wings have been struck down by the fall of a thunderbolt.
When this sovereign of the earth— whose footstool was made crimson by the mass of rays from the crest-jewels of the lords of men who were commanders of *akṣauhiṇī* armies—
fell to the ground, who would not have condemned a birth that is fragile and subject to the ruin of existence?
***** The Club-Fight // 3 // ***** When that lord of eleven armies had been struck down upon the earth,
the maiden Earth trembled, her girdle of rippling rivers shaking. Bhmj_10.86 //
The world became pervaded by hundreds of terrifying ill omens,
while the sky-dwellers proceeded, praising that battle.
Then Bhīma, treating the humiliation with contempt, touched with his foot the head of the Kuru lord, which was the very abode of the play of royal fortune.
Beholding the wheel-turning monarch fallen there like a god,
the earth wept with tears of pearls from necklaces broken by his trembling limbs.
Having repelled the roaring Bhīma, Dharmarāja said to Suyodhana:
"O King, this destruction of your friends is solely due to your own misconduct."
Seeing the head of the lord of the earth touched with his foot by Bhīma, he whose emblem was the palm tree, holding a raised plow and terrifying in his wrath, spoke: Bhāj 10.91.
Who, unless he were a beast, would touch with his foot the head of this man— who scorches his enemies with his majesty, who has seized the fortune of his foes, and who has struck off their heads?
Having spoken thus, the enemy of Kaṃsa pacified Bhīma, who was prepared to burn him with the fire of his wrath, by means of various words of conciliation.
To Kṛṣṇa, who was saying, "You are the power that neutralizes the evils of poison, lightning, and fire," Duryodhana spoke, having suppressed his intense pain.
"Having gained the confidence of the foolish cowherd boys, I have been deceived by you;
those heroes headed by Bhīṣma were struck down by you through mere stratagems."
I have eaten with friends, sported with beloveds, and offered oblations to the foremost of beings;
I have even met with death as befits a Kṣatriya—what other person is there who is my equal?
Enemies were driven into the forest depths by a mere frown of his brow with parched faces; Fortune herself was bestowed upon his foremost friends, adorned with smiles as bright as a turban-ornament;
even in battle he never turned his back, and his fame has taken root in all directions—what other desirable duty remains for him to perform that would be worthy of his life?
Having heard his words, the sons of Pṛthā, along with the kings, departed for victory, making the earth resound with their chariots as if they were proud men feeling ashamed.
Then, having set down Pradyumna, the first of the Phalgunas, Madhusūdana descended from the chariot; thereafter, that chariot burst into flames.
"This chariot, scorched by the weapons of Droṇa and Karṇa, is burning intensely," asked the astonished Pārtha; to him, the Slayer of Kāliya replied: Bhāj 10.100.
Having heard this terrible news from Sañjaya, the king, overwhelmed by delusion,
grieved for his sons while repeatedly remembering the words of Vidura.
Then, when the sage Kṛṣṇa had arrived at the Kuru palace, Hari,
having been dismissed by Ajātaśatru, approached and spoke to the king and Gāndhārī.
Though entreated for peace, the Kaurava did not desire it due to his own wicked conduct;
nor did the sons of Pṛthā deviate from righteousness, and thus he found no ground for his anger.
"Your sons, the sons of Pāṇḍu, possess the radiance of the gods today;
for it was said by you both previously: 'Where there is dharma, there is victory.'"
When those two Vṛṣṇi heroes had departed after thus propitiating him, and when the sage had consoled Ambikā’s son and departed, he questioned Sañjaya about what remained.
Then your son, being insulted on the surface of the earth, said to him:
"Look! I have been struck down by this cook through trickery."
In the meantime, the son of Droṇa, the son of Hṛdika, and the son of Gotama approached and beheld the lord of the Kauravas brought to such a state by Time.
Then the Guru’s son, wringing his hands together in anger and sighing, made a vow for the total destruction of all his enemies.
Then the king embraced that hero and made him his general;
for indeed, there is no loosening of the ego-sense even at the end for those possessed of self-conceit.
Having roared with a sound like the thundering of clouds at the end of an aeon, the son of Droṇa,
that king, fell into a precarious state of suffering during that night.
Then the sons of the preceptor Gautama Mahardikya entered the great forest,
perceiving within themselves the surging, wave-like instability of worldly splendor.
Thus ends the Gadāparvan in the Bhāratamañjarī composed by Kṣemendra.
